newsitem.title: USA: Talk of China cancellations hits US soymeal prices.
newsitem.headline: Talk of China cancellations hits US soymeal prices.

text.p: China has flexed its muscles in soymeal markets in recent days, using its status as a major buyer to cancel or switch its paper positions to meet its port problems and register handsome profits, grain traders said.
By cancelling or reselling soymeal purchase contracts this week, China can switch to cheaper forward positions and also cash in on paper gains from the recent rally, traders said.
"It does make sense. I can't tell you that I know for a fact there have been some cancellations but the mathematics would tell you that they would do that," a U.S. soy trader said.

Chicago Board of Trade soybean and soymeal futures fell on Friday on widespread talk that China had cancelled recent soymeal purchases of 450,000 tonnes, mostly from South America and India. China cancelled 48,000 tonnes in U.S. meal purchases three weeks ago.
CBOT March soymeal closed $1.80 a ton lower at $257.60 after trading as low as $255.50 early in the session.

Soymeal shipments into China have been backed up at Chinese ports by a lack of storage at ports, heavy arrivals and bad weather. Some of the meal is out in the open, leaving it exposed to the elements, Chinese traders said Thursday.
U.S. traders said China's soymeal demand outlook is still solid, based on its growing livestock and poultry industries.

But they said the port logjam and price differentials between suppliers in Brazil, Argentina, India and the U.S. had presented China's buyers with an opportunity to tweak their paper positions to posts gains as both buyers and sellers.

The U.S. soybean trader said, for instance, China probably bought Brazilian meal at $20 under March CBOT futures two months ago. He said the Brazilian spot market was now about even money with CBOT March and shipments for April would be about $13 under CBOT May.
"If you have a little excess inventory on hand and you don't really need it, sell it at even money, make $20 a ton and replace some at $13 a tonne under," the trader said.
"They have the best of both worlds," the soybean trader said. "Chinese buyers are (now) willing to purchase at $15 to $17 a ton under Brazil April FOB prices," he added.
Besides, the backwardation in CBOT futures makes a "sell-nearby, buy-forward" posture inviting for China.
While March CBOT soymeal closed at $257.60 on Friday, May futures ended at $251.90, July at $248.40 and August at $244.60.
One exporter said he believed the cancellations occurred sometime on Thursday and speculated with the Chinese domestic soymeal prices softening, nearby meal was not needed urgently.

"I don't think they cancelled that much," the U.S. exporter said of the rumors that China cancelled 450,000 tonnes. "But I know they cancelled one cargo from India of about 20,000 tonnes and they may have cancelled 100,000 tonnes of Brazilian meal."
"I'm not sure how much they cancelled but it is South American and Indian and not U.S.," another U.S. exporter said.
The cancellation by China of 48,000 tonnes of U.S. soymeal purchases reported by USDA on February 6 was the only formal cancellation of U.S. material by China in recent weeks.

In the USDA latest weekly export report issued Friday, in the week ended February 13, shipments of 48,200 tonnes to China were reported but cancellations to "unknown destinations" -- a category often signalling China -- totalled 71,400 tonnes.
Cancellations of soymeal sales to unknown destinations totalled 345,500 tonnes in the last five USDA weekly reports.
(Doris Frankel, 312-983-7305))
